name: stri_width
title: Determine the Width of Code Points

origin.description: Approximate how many columns a monospaced font would use to print each string.

arguments.name: str
arguments.text: A character vector, or an object coerced to character.

origin.details: General categories Me, Mn, Cf, and Cc have width 0, as do Hangul medial vowels, Hangul final consonants, and U+200B. East Asian wide and fullwidth characters have width 2. Most emoji and general category So have width 2. U+00AD has width 1. Everything else has width 1. A missing string stays missing.
origin.value: An integer vector the same length as str.
origin.example:
x <- stri_width(c(LETTERS[1:5], "\U0001F606", "\uFF21"))
cat(paste0("stri_width(c(LETTERS[1:5], \"\\U0001F606\", \"\\uFF21\")) returns ", paste(x, collapse = ", "), ".\n"))

translation.description: Approximate how many columns a monospaced font would use to print each string.

arguments.name: str
arguments.text: A string, NA, a number, a complex value, or a list of those. None is an empty vector.

translation.details: The same category and East Asian width rules as stringi 1.8.9. A regional-indicator pair contributes 2, and the next pair can start again. After U+200D, an emoji-presentation character or one of the gender and profession marks contributes 0. Unicode 16 marks and symbols that Python's unicodedata 15.1 does not list are included so the widths match ICU 76.
translation.value: An int, or NA. A list or tuple returns a list. None returns an empty list.
translation.example:
from stringi.length import stri_width
x = stri_width(list("ABCDE") + ["\U0001F606", "\uFF21"])
print("stri_width([\"A\", \"B\", \"C\", \"D\", \"E\", \"\\U0001F606\", \"\\uFF21\"]) returns " + ", ".join(str(value) for value in x) + ".")
